text: A superconducting quantum chip is useless at room temperature. It has to be cooled to a small fraction of a degree above absolute zero before it behaves like a quantum device at all — and the machine that gets it there is also one of the biggest hidden bottlenecks to scaling these systems up.

Millikelvin temperatures are non-negotiable for two separate reasons. First, the chip's aluminum or niobium circuitry actually has to be superconducting for the qubit to work, and superconductivity only kicks in below a material-specific critical temperature. Second, at any warmer temperature, the chip's surroundings contain enough ambient thermal microwave photons, close to the qubit's own operating frequency, to randomly kick it out of its ground state — which looks exactly like uncontrolled noise. Cooling to roughly 10 to 20 millikelvin suppresses that thermal photon population enough for the qubit to hold a controlled quantum state.

This is what that cooling machine actually looks like — a dilution refrigerator's staged, chandelier-like structure. Each gold plate you see is a colder stage than the one above it, nested like a set of thermally isolated shells, with the qubit chip itself mounted on the lowest, coldest plate.

No single cooling mechanism is efficient across the entire range from room temperature down to millikelvin, so the fridge cools in stages — each one removing the heat load appropriate to its own temperature range. The final, coldest stage is the mixing chamber, where a mixture of helium-3 and helium-4 spontaneously separates into two phases below a certain temperature. Continuously pumping helium-3 from the concentrated phase into the dilute phase absorbs heat, the same way evaporation does, except this process keeps working effectively all the way down to millikelvin. And here's the real engineering burden: every qubit typically needs its own microwave control and readout lines running from room temperature down through every one of those stages — which means a finite cryostat has a finite amount of space and a finite cooling budget for all that wiring.

Next lesson: the three companies that come up most often in superconducting quantum computing — IBM, Google, and Rigetti — and what each one is actually prioritizing with the hardware this chapter just explained.
